title: Your urge to breathe isn't about oxygen
topic: What happens to your body when you hold your breath?

beats.label: breath hold
lines: Your urge to breathe isn't mainly about running out of oxygen.
The alarm comes mainly from rising carbon dioxide levels.

beats.label: of oxygen at rest goes to the brain
lines: Meanwhile, your brain uses about twenty percent of your oxygen at rest, with little in reserve.

beats.title: Before a dive
lines: Here's the trap: breathing fast and deep before a dive lowers carbon dioxide, delaying the warning.
So the brain can feel comfortable while oxygen drops to dangerous levels.

beats.sub: most likely on the way up
lines: Blackouts are most likely on the way up, can strike within seconds, and may come with no urgent urge to breathe.

beats.title: Who blacks out?
lines: And the victims are often fit, strong swimmers who had done many dives without problems.
So never breathe fast and deep before going under, and always dive with a buddy watching from the surface.

sources.claim: The urge to breathe is primarily driven by rising carbon dioxide levels rather than falling oxygen levels.
The brain uses about 20% of the oxygen under resting conditions but has low reserves.
Hyperventilation before a dive reduces carbon dioxide, delays the warning signals to breathe and can mislead the brain into feeling comfortable while oxygen drops to dangerous levels.
Blackouts are more likely during ascent, can occur within seconds, and happen when the swimmer does not necessarily feel an urgent need to breathe.
Victims are often established breath-hold divers who are fit, strong swimmers and have completed many dives before without problems.
Freedivers are strongly advised not to hyperventilate and are encouraged to dive only with a buddy observing from the surface.

youtube.title: Your urge to breathe isn't about oxygen 🫁
youtube.description: Holding your breath sets off a carbon dioxide alarm, not an oxygen one, and that is why breathing fast before a dive is so risky.
